verdict: This is a well-written syllabus that is not yet a German one. The cultural and register work is genuinely strong – Danke meaning 'no thanks', halb fünf, the Sie/duzen negotiation, Pfand and cash, Austrian and Bavarian variants, the dative-feelings frame, kein vs nicht, the Perfekt as the spoken past – and the notes are the best thing in it. But structurally it is a Hindi syllabus wearing German clothes, and it shows in three ways. First, waste: roughly one card in ten is a duplicate of another (three Wurst cards, three kochen, three also, three Straßenbahn, three Perfekt paradigms, two each of Kaffee, Handy, Heizung, Tante, Vielen Dank, Was kostet das?, auf, hinter, halb, null, werden, fahren), often at conflicting tiers, which in an SRS means near-identical cards colliding in review for no gain. Second, leakage: dozens of learner-facing notes still explain German by reference to dal, chai, mithai, mango, biryani, thali, kurta, khichdi, kal and साला, and four of them ("the spine's loan doublet", "the spine's native/loan pair collapses here", "slot reused") leak internal pipeline jargon straight to the learner. Third, and most serious, the shape of the language it teaches is the shape of Hindi's needs rather than German's: the two highest-frequency German prepositions, zu and an, have no card at all while "zu = closed" sits at tier 2; sein has a full present paradigm but haben has none; essen, kennen, bleiben, finden, dürfen and sollen exist only inside other cards' notes; there is no verb-second rule, no zu-infinitive or um…zu, no participle-formation rule, no strong-verb vowel change, no reflexive paradigm, no genitive and no Präteritum despite reading being a stated goal; and not one card maps German spelling to sound (ei/ie – Wein vs Wien – w/v/z, final -er, -ig), the first thing a British learner gets wrong and precisely what a Devanagari-derived spine would never think to include because its learners got romanisation for free. The work strand, the learner's stated first priority, is the thinnest of all: Kollege, Chef, Termin, Besprechung, E-Mail, Feierabend, Mittagspause, sich krankmelden and the email sign-offs are all absent, as are Prost, Bier, Guten Tag, Auf Wiedersehen, Zusammen oder getrennt?, Zahlen bitte and buchstabieren. Cut the duplicates, de-Hindi the notes, add the sixty-odd items below, and it becomes a genuinely good German syllabus – the raw material is there.

Batterie is only the disposable sort. Akku ist alle = battery's gone.
Ich habe kein Netz = I've no signal. Empfang is also a hotel reception.
Pronounced as in English, but feminine: die DB-App.
Say ON-line. Ich bestelle das online.
Verbindung also means a train connection.
The standard sign-off in work and private life; Melde dich mal! = do get in touch.
Air conditioning is rare; lüften (airing the room daily, windows wide) is the national habit instead.
Mist! = damn. Um Gottes willen for something serious.
Literally 'madness'; used for good and bad news alike.
Kein Ding / Passiert. = no worries, it happens.

items.en: just like that, for no reason
items.note: Warum? – Einfach so.
Passt schon in the south and Austria, where it also means 'never mind'. Alles klar does the same job everywhere.
Gefunden! works too. Hab's kapiert = I've understood.
eine Million = a million. The real false friend is die Billion, which is a British trillion (10¹²); a British billion (10⁹) is eine Milliarde.

The German respect ritual: a firm handshake with eye contact when you first meet someone, and again when you are introduced to a new colleague. No hugging with anyone you Sie. Regulars just say Morgen.
der Dom = cathedral. Kirchensteuer is deducted from salaries if you register as a member.
Ich ärgere mich über ... . Er ist sauer = he's cross.
Ich habe Angst vor Hunden – vor + dative.
lächeln = to smile.
sich ändern = to change in nature; umsteigen = change trains.
Also Ist schon gut. Lass mal! when someone reaches for the bill.
singen = to sing; der Song for pop music.
allein is simply on your own and carries no sadness.
Shrugging. Mal sehen = we'll see.
Taxis run on a metered fare by law – no negotiating. Ask for a Quittung if you need the receipt.
vier → vierte, zwanzig → zwanzigste. Irregular: erste, dritte, siebte, achte.
dreiviertel sechs = 5:45 in Saxony, Bavaria and Austria. Everywhere else: Viertel vor sechs.
Wait for green even on an empty street – Germans do, especially with children about.
112 for ambulance and fire, 110 for police, anywhere in the EU.
Wir möchten bestellen. Also for online orders.
Links abbiegen, an der Ampel rechts abbiegen.

items.word: der Mann, der ... / die Frau, die ...
items.roman: der Mann, der ... / die Frau, die ...
items.note: Same forms as the article, and the verb goes to the end: Das ist der Zug, der nach Berlin fährt. Essential for reading.
Das geht schon / Passt scho in the south.
Resigned shrug. Da kann man nichts machen.
benützen in the south. verwenden is a touch more formal.
Phone numbers: null-eins-sieben-null.
German writes numbers as one word, however long: zweihundertfünfunddreißig.
Schönes Wochenende! is the Friday goodbye in every office.

items.word: am ersten Mai / am zweiten Mai
items.roman: am ersten Mai / am zweiten Mai
items.note: Written 1.5. or 01.05.2026 – day first, always. Der wievielte ist heute? – Der erste.
Jänner in Austria.
Often said Feb-RU-ar; Feber in parts of Austria.
Der 1. Mai is a public holiday everywhere.
On the phone Germans say Juno to keep it apart from Juli.
Said Julei when clarity matters.
Stress the second syllable: au-GUST.
The Oktoberfest starts in September.
With mein it means partner; without it, ein Freund von mir is just a friend. Partner/Partnerin is the neutral option.
sich verloben = to get engaged.
das Brautpaar = the couple.
ältere Menschen is the polite everyday phrase; alte Leute sounds blunt.
in Rente gehen = to retire. Rentner is neutral and not a slight; ältere Menschen is the polite way to talk about older people generally.
Reinigungskraft is the neutral, official word.
gebrochen = broken: Der Arm ist gebrochen.
Probier mal! anprobieren = to try clothes on; versuchen = to attempt.
Ein Pfund Hackfleisch, bitte. Still normal at markets and butchers, and it is exactly half a kilo.
der Backofen = oven.
Brauchen Sie eine Tüte? – they cost money. Sackerl in Austria; bring a Stoffbeutel.
Rare in homes and older offices; Germans open the windows instead.
Die Heizung aufdrehen = turn the heating up.
der Schweiß = sweat.

items.en: to get on, to get in
items.note: The trio you hear on every platform: einsteigen, aussteigen, umsteigen (change trains).
Moin (north, any time of day), Grüß Gott (Bavaria and Austria), Servus (both hello and bye in the south).
Only for going to bed. Leaving in the evening: Schönen Abend noch! Schlaf gut = sleep well.
Heard at every bakery and bar counter. At home a host asks Was möchtest du trinken?
Es ist ewig her! = it's been ages.
Kein Stress! / Locker bleiben. Stress is fully naturalised: Ich habe Stress.
Wir vermissen dich – vermissen takes the accusative. Du fehlst mir turns it round: literally 'you are missing to me'.
What people actually say is Ich habe gerade viel zu tun or Ich bin im Stress.

items.en: to be free, to have time
items.note: Hast du kurz Zeit? = have you got a moment? Ich habe frei = I'm off work.
Fully naturalised (say DSCHOP). die Stelle = a position; der Beruf = profession, asked as Was machen Sie beruflich?
studieren = to be at university, not 'to study for a test' – that's lernen.
Short for Universität. There is no 'college'; Hochschule and Fachhochschule are the other institutions.
Say ZEH-ri-e. der Tatort on Sunday nights is the shared national one.
Das Spiel läuft gerade. Also a game or play generally; spielen = to play.
die Nachrichten = the news; die Tagesschau at 8pm is the institution everyone means.
Krankenhaus for hospital generally; Klinik for a specialist one; der Notarzt is the emergency doctor.
Say KNEE with the k sounded: k-nie.
Halt mal kurz = hold this a second. Der Zug hält hier nicht. Irregular: hält, hielt, gehalten.
Er ist hingefallen – takes sein. Something dropping is runtergefallen.
Soll ich dir nachschenken? = shall I top you up? German has no causative 'make someone drink'.
Ich helfe jemandem, ich sehe jemanden. Also niemandem/niemanden for nobody.
Er ist wohl schon weg = he must have left already. This is how German guesses – present tense plus wohl, no special form.

items.en: about to: present tense + gleich (in a moment)
items.note: Ich gehe gleich los = I'm about to leave. Ich wollte gerade gehen = I was just about to go. There is no separate 'going to' form.
Iss mal ordentlich. Also 'tidy': ein ordentliches Zimmer.
doch is the nudge that makes an invitation warm rather than flat.

items.word: Sag Bescheid, wenn du da bist.
items.roman: Sag Bescheid, wenn du da bist.
items.en: let me know when you get there
items.note: Bescheid sagen/geben = to let someone know – one of the most useful German phrases there is.
Super! and Bravo! also work; Respekt! for something impressive.
Same word for sugar-sweet and for a lovely child. niedlich = cute of animals and small things.
Shoes come off at the door and guests are offered these. Schlappen colloquially; Pantoffeln old-fashioned.
Frohe Ostern! The other fixtures you'll be wished on: Weihnachten, Silvester, Karneval/Fasching.
der Reisepass = passport. Germans carry a Personalausweis and officials ask for it routinely.
Hast du das gecheckt? Spoken German borrows English verbs and conjugates them flat out: gegoogelt, gedownloadet, geliked.
Du bist auf Lautsprecher = you're on speaker.
der Jahrestag for anniversaries generally.
Singular in German: Wo ist meine Brille? Sonnenbrille for sunglasses.

items.en: ei says "eye", ie says "ee": Wein (wine) vs Wien (Vienna)
items.note: The pair is pronounced like the English name of its SECOND letter. drei, nein, heißen, weiß vs vier, sieben, Bier, wie. Get this wrong and you order wine in the capital of Austria.

items.word: w = v, v = f, z = ts, s = z
items.roman: w = v, v = f, z = ts, s = z
items.note: Wasser = "vasser", Vater = "fahter", zehn = "tsayn", sagen = "zahgen". At the start of a word st- and sp- are "sht-" and "shp-": Straße, sprechen, Sport.

items.en: final -er is a vowel; final -ig sounds like -ich
items.note: Vater ≈ "FAH-tuh", Kinder ≈ "KIN-duh", aber ≈ "AH-buh" – no British r at the end. zwanzig, richtig and billig end in the ich sound (the south says -ik).

items.en: the umlauts, and why they matter
items.note: ä ≈ the e in "bed"; ö = say "eh" with rounded lips; ü = say "ee" with rounded lips. They change the word: schon (already) vs schön (nice), Mutter vs Mütter, Bruder vs Brüder.

items.en: verb second: whatever comes first, the verb still comes second
items.note: Ich fahre morgen nach Wien = Morgen fahre ich nach Wien. Put a time or a place first and the subject hops behind the verb. This one rule does more for sounding German than any amount of vocabulary.
ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. Speech drops the -e: ich hab. It also builds most of the past tense, so it earns its keep twice over.
Vowel-changing: ich esse, du isst, er isst. Perfekt: Ich hab schon gegessen. Tablets are nehmen, never essen.
zu + Dativ, contracting to zum / zur: zum Arzt, zur Arbeit, zum Bahnhof, zu mir. Towns and countries take nach (nach Wien), going inside a building takes in (ins Büro).
an der Wand, am Bahnhof, am Montag, am Abend, am Telefon. an + Akkusativ for movement: Ich häng das Bild an die Wand. One of the five prepositions you cannot get through a day without.

items.en: two-way prepositions: accusative for movement, dative for position
items.note: in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen. Wohin? takes the accusative (ins Büro, auf den Tisch), wo? the dative (im Büro, auf dem Tisch).

items.word: du sprichst / er nimmt / er fährt
items.roman: du sprichst / er nimmt / er fährt
items.en: strong verbs change their vowel in the du and er forms
items.note: e → i/ie: sprechen, nehmen, geben, essen, sehen, lesen, helfen. a → ä: fahren, schlafen, halten, tragen. Only those two forms change – wir and ihr stay regular.

items.en: how the Partizip II is built
items.note: Weak: ge- + stem + -t. Strong: ge- + stem + -en, often with a new vowel. NO ge- on verbs in -ieren (telefoniert, reserviert) or with be-, ver-, er-, ent- (bezahlt, verstanden). Separables wrap it: angerufen, aufgemacht.
ich darf, du darfst, er darf. Darf ich? asks permission. Prohibition is nicht dürfen: Hier darf man nicht rauchen. Careful – nicht müssen means you don't have to, not that you mustn't.
Soll ich uns einen Kaffee machen? is the standard offer. Du solltest zum Arzt gehen = you ought to see a doctor. Ich soll das machen = I've been told to.
"Du kommst nicht?" – "Doch!" English has no word for this and Brits reliably miss it. Inside a sentence it nudges: Komm doch mit, Bleib doch zum Essen.
Ich hab schon gegessen. Warst du schon mal in Wien? = have you ever been. Also a softener: Das passt schon, Das wird schon.
Noch ein Bier, bitte = another beer. Noch nicht = not yet. Bist du noch da? = are you still there? Sonst noch was? = anything else?

items.en: reflexive verbs: mich, dich, sich, uns, euch
items.note: German uses far more of them than English: sich treffen, sich beeilen, sich freuen, sich ärgern, sich erkälten. Accusative normally (Ich freu mich), dative when there is already an object (Ich wasch mir die Hände).

items.en: in order to; and the zu-infinitive
items.note: Ich fahr nach Wien, um Kollegen zu treffen. After vergessen, versuchen, anfangen, Lust haben, Zeit haben: Ich hab vergessen, dich anzurufen – zu slots inside a separable verb.

items.en: endings that give a noun's gender away
items.note: die: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -ie. das: -chen, -lein, -ment, and any infinitive used as a noun (das Essen). der: -er, -ling, -ismus, plus days, months and weather. The rest you learn with the article attached.
Ich komm nicht, denn ich bin krank – no verb to the end, unlike weil. denn is also the question softener that makes you sound native: Was machst du denn? Wo bist du denn?
Nicht heute, sondern morgen. If the first half is negative and you are correcting it, German needs sondern – aber is wrong there and marks you out instantly.
Verb to the end: Ich geh hin, obwohl ich müde bin. In a main clause the same job is done by trotzdem.

items.word: des Chefs / der Firma / wegen des Wetters
items.roman: des Chefs / der Firma / wegen des Wetters
items.en: the genitive – mostly a reading skill
items.note: Masculine and neuter add -(e)s: das Auto des Chefs. Feminine and plural just take der. Speech says von dem Chef, but contracts, signs, headlines and any book you pick up use it constantly.

items.en: Präteritum: the past tense of written German
items.note: Novels, news and reports use it where speech uses the Perfekt. Weak verbs add -te (machte, sagte, wohnte); strong verbs change vowel (ging, kam, gab, fand, sprach, schrieb). You need to recognise it, not produce it.
Die Tür wird um acht geschlossen. Past: wurde. Signs, instructions and news run on it; speech usually dodges it with man: Das macht man so.

Weak masculine: mit dem Kollegen, die Kollegen. Freund means friend or partner, so a workmate is always Kollege – the single most-needed noun for this learner and it currently lives only inside another card's note.
False friend: nothing to do with cooking (that's der Koch). Use it about the person, but address them as Herr or Frau + surname like everyone else.
German life runs on these: Ich hab um drei einen Termin. einen Termin machen / absagen / verschieben. Turning up without one is often simply not possible.
das Meeting is used just as much in offices; die Sitzung is the formal one. Ich bin gerade in einer Besprechung.
Feminine, and the hyphen is standard. Ich schick dir eine Mail. Work German also says: Ich setz dich in CC.
The everyday close. Mit freundlichen Grüßen is the formal one, Liebe Grüße (LG) the warm one. Openers: Hallo Frau Weber, or Sehr geehrte Frau Weber when it needs to be formal.

items.en: the end of the working day
items.note: Ich mach Feierabend = I'm knocking off. Schönen Feierabend! is the standard five o'clock goodbye. Germans mean it – nobody expects a reply after it.
Gehen wir zusammen essen? is how colleagues arrange it. Many offices eat early, from about half twelve, and actually leave the desk.
Ich muss mich krankmelden. From about day three you need a Krankschreibung from a doctor: Ich bin krankgeschrieben.
Said to every colleague on a Friday. The reply is Danke, dir auch! or Ihnen auch!

items.word: Ich hätte da mal eine Frage.
items.roman: Ich hätte da mal eine Frage.
items.note: The soft way to interrupt a colleague. Hast du kurz? = have you got a second?
Mensa at a university. Was gibt's heute? is what you ask on the way in.
Safe with anyone you Sie, from mid-morning on. Guten Morgen before that, Guten Abend from about six. Grüß Gott in Bavaria and Austria, Moin in the north.
Shops, offices, officials, doctors. On the phone it is Auf Wiederhören – you say hearing, not seeing.
Clink with each person in turn and look them in the eye as you do it – skipping the eye contact is genuinely rude. Zum Wohl! is the wine and southern version.
Ein großes / kleines Bier, bitte. Ein Helles in Bavaria, ein Kölsch in Cologne, ein Pils in the north. Ein Radler is beer with lemonade; the no-alcohol one is ein alkoholfreies.
You will be asked this every single time. Getrennt, bitte – and German splitting really is per item, not per head.
You pay the waiter at the table, not at a till, and you flag them down to do it. Die Rechnung, bitte works too.
Round up by 5-10% and say the total out loud as you hand the money over: "Machen Sie 20" on an 18.40 bill. Stimmt so = keep the change. Coins left on the table is not the custom.
You will need it for names, streets and email addresses. Learn your own name in German letters: v is "fau", w is "veh", j is "jott", y is "Ypsilon", ß is "Eszett", and ä/ö/ü are "a/o/u Umlaut".
mit dem Rad fahren = to cycle. Cycle lanes are often part of the pavement, and standing in one gets you a bell rung at you.

items.en: deposit on a bottle or can
items.note: 25 cents on most plastic bottles and cans, less on reusable glass, more on a crate. You feed them into the Pfandautomat at the supermarket and get a voucher for the till.
Signage you read rather than say. Ausfahrt is a road exit, Notausgang the emergency one, Zutritt verboten means keep out.
Rauchen verboten, Betreten verboten, Parken verboten. German signs state the rule flatly; it reads harsher in English than it is meant.
Signs and announcements: Achtung, Türen schließen selbsttätig. Vorsicht! is what you shout at a person.
Shops shut completely, exactly like a Sunday, and the dates differ by Bundesland – Bavaria and Austria have the most. Brückentag is the bridging day everyone books off.
Hotel check-in. They will ask Auf welchen Namen? and then for your Ausweis or Reisepass.
One of the most-said words in spoken German: Was machst du eigentlich beruflich? Eigentlich schon = well, yes, sort of. It softens a question into small talk.
The classic British trap: it never means "become" (that is werden). Ich hab deine Mail bekommen. Spoken alternative: kriegen.
False friend – never "eventually", which is schließlich or irgendwann. Written evtl.
Another false friend – "actually" is eigentlich or tatsächlich. Die aktuelle Version, aktuelle Zahlen.

items.en: to know (a person, a place, a thing)
items.note: Ich kenn ihn / die Stadt / das Lokal. Facts take wissen: Ich weiß, wo er wohnt. kennenlernen = to meet for the first time.
Ich bleib zu Hause. Perfekt with sein: Ich bin da geblieben. Bleib gesund! is a normal sign-off.
Ich find das gut is how Germans give an opinion, more often than Ich denke. Also literal: Ich find meinen Schlüssel nicht.

items.en: to be standing / to be lying (where a thing is)
items.note: German says how a thing sits: Die Flasche steht auf dem Tisch, das Buch liegt daneben. The action pair is stellen and legen.
Separable: Hör auf! Es hat aufgehört zu regnen. Vehicles stop with halten or anhalten instead.
Dative for the person: Ich antworte dir. auf + Akkusativ for the question. beantworten takes a plain object: eine Frage beantworten, eine Mail beantworten.
Es schneit = it's snowing. glatt = icy underfoot, Winterreifen are legally required in the conditions, and Austrian trains keep running regardless.
The two colours missing from the set. grau is what Germans call the whole winter sky, and half the bread is braun.
